meta.title: Who really said "Find the good. It's all around you. Find it, showcase it and you'll start believing in it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Jesse Owens really wrote it — page 166 of his 1970 book Blackthink, chapter 8, “Showcase the Good.” The line you see online is cut short.

meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Jesse Owens. Quote Investigator pins it to page 166 of Blackthink (William Morrow, 1970) — and the passage keeps going after the famous part.

source.excerpt:
Find the good. It’s all around you. Find it, showcase it and you’ll start believing in it. And so will most of the people who come into contact with you.
Showcase the good. Believe in it. It’s real, baby.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traced the line to Owens’s own book, citing Blackthink: My Life as Black Man and White Man by Jesse Owens with Paul G. Neimark (William Morrow and Company, New York, 1970), chapter 8, “Showcase the Good,” page 166, and concluding that Owens “deserves credit for this remark which he included in his 1970 book Blackthink.”

The book is exactly what that citation describes: the Open Library edition record ↗ gives Morrow, New York, 1970, 215 pages, by-statement “[by] Jesse Owens, with Paul G. Neimark” — so a page 166 exists — and a scanned copy ↗ is catalogued at the Internet Archive under both authors.

Quote Investigator also records the sentence being reprinted in 1993 with its Blackthink credit still attached — Dorothy Winbush Riley’s collection My Soul Looks Back, ‘Less I Forget prints it on page 31 over the credit line “JESSE OWENS, Blackthink, 1970” — and again in 1995, when syndicated columnist Larry Meeks ran it as a “Notable Quote” in The Modesto Bee of 19 May credited to Owens alone — see the exhibit ↗.

Worth knowing where it is not: Wikiquote’s Jesse Owens page ↗ carries a sourced quotation from Blackthink (1970) but does not list this one at all — part of why the line spread with no citation attached.
source.excerptNote: The passage as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from page 166. The version that circulates online stops after “believing in it” — the sentences that follow, including the chapter’s own title phrase, are almost never carried with it.

author.name: Jesse Owens
author.heading: Who Jesse Owens was
author.metaLine: 1913–1980 · American sprinter, four-time Olympic gold medallist & author
author.bio: James Cleveland “Jesse” Owens was born in Oakville, Alabama in 1913 and won four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics — 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump and 4×100-metre relay. The medals did not translate into a career: he worked for decades as a public-relations businessman, sports promoter and speaker, and served as a US goodwill ambassador from 1955. He was also a writer, publishing Blackthink in 1970 and I Have Changed in 1972 with the collaborator Paul G. Neimark; he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1976 and died in Tucson, Arizona in 1980.

misattribution.heading: Not the wrong man — the wrong half of the sentence
misattribution.intro: This is an unusual case for a famous name: the attribution is right. Jesse Owens really did write it. What goes wrong is everything around the words — the source vanishes, the passage gets cut, and the line gets read as a track-and-field motto when it comes from a book about race in America.

items.why: The line sits in BrainyQuote’s Jesse Owens list ↗ with no book, no chapter and no page beside it — the same bare presentation that usually signals a fabrication. Here the citation existed all along; it simply was not carried. Quote Investigator supplied it: Blackthink, page 166.

The popular quotation ends at “believing in it.” On the page it keeps going — “And so will most of the people who come into contact with you. Showcase the good. Believe in it. It’s real, baby” — per Quote Investigator’s transcription ↗. The cut drops the point Owens was building to: that showcasing the good is what persuades everyone else, not just you.

items.who: Readers who take it as an athlete’s training maxim
items.why: Owens’s four gold medals make the line read like locker-room advice. It is not from a sports memoir: QI places it ↗ in chapter 8 of Blackthink, a chapter titled “Showcase the Good,” in a 1970 book about Owens’s life as a Black man in America.

A similar-sounding saying is not Owens’s and has its own history: Quote Investigator ↗ found its earliest exact match in an 1896 report by Madison Babcock on the public schools of San Francisco — “Find the good and praise it, speak sparingly of the bad” — and tentatively credits him. Two different lines; don’t merge them.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is genuinely Owens’s own writing: page 166 of Blackthink (1970), in a chapter he called “Showcase the Good” — Quote Investigator’s citation ↗.

context.heading: Why he was writing it
lead: Blackthink: My Life as Black Man and White Man, written with Paul G. Neimark and published by William Morrow in 1970, was Owens’s argument against what he saw as the destructive turn in Black politics at the end of the 1960s. The chapter this sentence comes from — “Showcase the Good” — is where he sets out the alternative he believed in.

The advice is practical rather than sentimental. Owens is not claiming the good is easy to see; he is claiming that belief follows attention, and that other people’s belief follows yours. That is exactly what the truncated version loses, because the rest of the passage is about the effect on everyone else in the room.

The book was not his last word. In 1972 Owens published I Have Changed, in which, as Wikipedia notes ↗, he revised the positions on Black activism he had taken earlier. This sentence outlived that revision in public memory — as did one other line from the same book, the “battles that count” passage Wikiquote carries ↗.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s exhibit shows the quotation moving with its citation intact for a while. It appears in Dorothy Winbush Riley’s 1993 anthology My Soul Looks Back, ‘Less I Forget: A Collection of Quotations by People of Color on page 31, credited to Jesse Owens, Blackthink, 1970.

In 1995 the syndicated columnist Larry Meeks ran it as a “Notable Quote” in The Modesto Bee of 19 May and credited Owens. Somewhere between those reprints and the modern quote-aggregator listings the book title fell away — which is how a properly sourced sentence ends up looking like an internet-manufactured one.
QI credits the reader inquiry that prompted the investigation to Schuyler W. Huck.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the line originated with Jesse Owens in his 1970 book Blackthink, citing chapter 8 “Showcase the Good” page 166, quoting the fuller passage ending “It's real, baby”; bibliographic line “Blackthink: My Life as Black Man and White Man by Jesse Owens With Paul G. Neimark, William Morrow and Company, New York”; also cites the 1993 Dorothy Winbush Riley collection (p. 31) and columnist Larry Meeks in The Modesto Bee, 19 May 1995; acknowledgement to Schuyler W. Huck.

Quote Investigator tentatively credits “Find the good and praise it” to Madison Babcock, earliest exact match an 1896 annual report on the public schools of San Francisco: “Find the good and praise it, speak sparingly of the bad.”

The Internet Archive holds a scan of Blackthink; my life as black man and white man, creators Owens, Jesse, 1913- and Neimark, Paul G, publisher New York, Morrow, 1970, LCCN 73106343, flagged as an access-restricted item.
